Besnagar Inscription
------------------------------------------
Inscription on stone pillars and walls as also on metal plates have always been a source of valuable material for reconstructing ancient or medieval Indian history. One such, belonging to a fairly early period (2nd century B.C.) is the बेस्नगर् इन्स्च्रिप्तिओन्, discovered on a ‘garuḍadhvaja’ (votive pillar with the sculpture of गरुड, the mythical bird-mount of विष्णु) near Bhilsa in Madhya Pradesh.
Besnagar was the capital of the Śuṅga dynasty which ruled during the period 187-75 B.C.
The stone pillar has been dedicated to वासुदेव (Kṛṣṇa), called ‘deva-deva’ or ‘God of gods’, by हेलिओदोरोस् who was a Yavana or a Greek. In the inscription on it, he calls himself as a ‘paramabhāgavata’ (the best of the bhāgavatas or devotees of विष्णु). He was the son of one Diya and a native of तक्षशिला. He had been deputed as the ambassador by the Greek king Antialcidas to the Indian king भग-bhadra Kāśīputra, probably the same as the fifth Śuṅga king Bhadraka.
This inscription proves two things, viz., that the कृष्ण-वासुदेव cult or the भागवत religion had already become quite popular and that even Greeks of high descent had gladly accepted it. Incidentally, this also helps us to prove the historicity of कृष्ण.
